name: Kobe
tagline: A city where harbor, foreign-style mansions and night views line up along a single axis
intro: Stretched out between the mountains and the sea, this port city links the night views of Meriken Park, the Western-style mansions of the Kitano hills and the street-food lanes of Nankinmachi on foot. Arima Onsen beyond the mountains, the Mt. Rokko and Mt. Maya night views and Himeji Castle, 40 minutes away by Special Rapid train, are all easy day trips. Two nights covers the essentials, and three nights lets you fit in both the hot springs and the castle. With Kobe beef, Western-style dining and desserts, it suits two women traveling together and families with children alike.
season_notes: Spring (Mar-May): cherry blossoms at Himeji Castle peak in early April, and the weather is at its best for strolling Kitano and Meriken Park. Summer (Jun-Aug): hot and humid after the rainy season; the top of Mt. Rokko is 5 to 7 degrees cooler than downtown, making it a summer retreat, and there are harbor fireworks in early August (to be confirmed). Autumn (Oct-Nov): the maples at Zuihoji Park and on Mt. Rokko peak in mid to late November, which is also high season for Arima Onsen. Winter (Dec-Feb): the Kobe Luminarie in December (to be confirmed) and the clear air make the night views sharpest; it is below freezing up in the mountains.
airport_access/0/note: Boarding area on the 1st floor of Terminal 1, every 20 to 30 minutes during the daytime. ¥2,200 is the fare after the 2024 increase (to be confirmed)
airport_access/1/note: 30 min by boat (¥1,880) + 18 min on the Port Liner (¥340). A discounted Bay Shuttle fare for foreign visitors may be available (to be confirmed). The bus is easier if you have a lot of luggage
airport_access/2/mode: JR Kansai Airport Rapid + Special Rapid (transfer at Osaka)
airport_access/2/note: Change trains at Osaka Station. Cheap, but you have to transfer with your luggage
airport_access/3/note: Driverless train that connects directly to the arrivals floor. ¥340 is the fare as of 2024 (to be confirmed). The front seat is the best spot
getting_around: The main areas (Sannomiya, Motomachi, Meriken Park, Harborland and Kitano) all fit within 2 km east to west and 1.5 km north to south, so walking or hopping one or two stops on the Kaigan Line subway is enough. Kitano is uphill, so take the City Loop bus up and walk back down. For Arima, take the express bus from Sannomiya Bus Terminal; for Mt. Rokko, take a bus and cable car from Hankyu Rokko Station; for Himeji, use the JR Special Rapid; and for the airport, use the limousine bus.
transport_pass: If you ride all the transport on Mt. Rokko and Mt. Maya (cable cars, ropeways and mountaintop buses) in one day, the Rokko-Maya Leisure Ticket (around ¥2,000 for the Hankyu version, to be confirmed) is a good deal. In the city, tapping a transit card (Suica or ICOCA) is more convenient, and the City Loop bus one-day pass (around ¥700, to be confirmed) only pays off if you ride up the Kitano hill three or more times.
spots/0/desc: Kansai's main gateway, with the most direct flights from Incheon, Gimhae (Busan), Daegu and other cities. The easiest way to reach Sannomiya in Kobe with no transfers is the limousine bus from the 1st-floor bus stop.
spots/0/access: Board the bus bound for Kobe Sannomiya at the limousine bus stop on the 1st floor. The Bay Shuttle ferry leaves from the pier near Terminal 2
spots/0/hours: International terminal open around the clock
spots/0/tip: For the limousine bus, buy your ticket first with cash or a card (a transit card is not accepted). For departures, arriving 2 hours before is enough.
spots/0/kid_tip: If your child gets carsick on buses, the Bay Shuttle (30 minutes by boat) plus the Port Liner (driverless train) is more fun.
spots/1/desc: A small airport on an artificial island in the bay, which began receiving international charter flights in 2025. It connects straight to the Port Liner from the arrivals floor, and Sannomiya is only 18 minutes away.
spots/1/access: Directly connected to Kobe Airport Station on the Port Liner. 18 minutes to Sannomiya, ¥340 (to be confirmed)
spots/1/tip: Even if you fly in direct to Kansai Airport, taking the Bay Shuttle on the way back (the pier is next to Kobe Airport) lets you link the Port Liner, the boat and the airport in one smooth line.
spots/1/kid_tip: The Port Liner has no driver's cab, so if your child sits in the front seat, it feels like they are driving the train themselves.
spots/2/desc: Kobe's central station, where JR, Hankyu, Hanshin, the subway and the Port Liner all meet. The limousine buses and the buses to Arima Onsen also leave from the bus terminal on the east side of the station, so it is the starting point for every day.
spots/2/access: JR Sannomiya Station, Hankyu Kobe-Sannomiya Station and Subway Sannomiya Station are linked underground and by elevated decks
spots/2/tip: The stations are scattered by company, which is confusing at first. Use the JR Central Exit as your reference point from your hotel.
spots/2/kid_tip: The arcades connect the underground passages and Center Gai, so you can get around with a stroller even on rainy days.
spots/3/desc: A Sanyo Shinkansen station, 2 minutes from Sannomiya by subway. Right behind the station are the Nunobiki Herb Garden ropeway station and the entrance to the Nunobiki Falls walking trail.
spots/3/access: One stop from Sannomiya Station on the Seishin-Yamate Subway Line, 2 minutes, ¥210 (to be confirmed)
spots/3/tip: You also take the Shinkansen from this station when heading on to Kyoto or Hiroshima. The ropeway station is a 5-minute walk along the road behind the station's 1st floor.
spots/4/desc: A wide lawn park facing the harbor, where the white BE KOBE letters are Kobe's signature photo spot. Port Tower, the Maritime Museum and Hotel Okura are all in one area, making it a good starting point for an evening stroll.
spots/4/access: 15-minute walk from JR/Hanshin Motomachi Station, 8-minute walk from Minatomotomachi Station on the Kaigan Subway Line
spots/4/tip: Arrive before sunset, take your BE KOBE photo, then walk to Port Tower and on to Harborland to see both the sunset and the night view in one go.
spots/4/kid_tip: It is wide and flat, so children can run around freely. You can also see part of the pier left as a reminder of the 1995 earthquake.
spots/5/desc: A red steel tower with a narrow waist, which gained an open-air rooftop deck after its 2024 renovation. You can see Mt. Rokko on one side and the sea and the Harborland Ferris wheel on the other, so Kobe's geography unfolds at a glance.
spots/5/access: In Meriken Park, 5-minute walk from Minatomotomachi Station on the subway
spots/5/tip: ¥1,000 for the observation floors only, ¥1,200 including the rooftop deck (to be confirmed). The best time to go in is 30 minutes before sunset.
spots/5/kid_tip: Part of the observation floor has a glass section. If your child is scared, just keep them by the windows.
spots/6/desc: Kobe's largest commercial complex, with the seaside Mosaic shopping mall and a big Ferris wheel side by side. At night the wheel's lights change, and the spot facing Port Tower across the water is the classic Kobe night view.
spots/6/access: 8-minute walk from JR Kobe Station, 10-minute walk from Meriken Park (across the bridge)
spots/6/tip: Many shops close at 20:00, so if you want to shop, do it first and have dinner afterward. The Ferris wheel costs around ¥800 per person (to be confirmed).
spots/6/kid_tip: One turn of the Ferris wheel takes about 10 minutes, and the cabins are enclosed, so even young children are fine. Many restaurants on the 2nd floor of Mosaic have kids' chairs.
spots/7/desc: A dozen or so Western-style mansions built by foreign merchants after the port opened are gathered on the hillside. Each mansion has its own admission, but just walking the lanes and admiring the exteriors gives you plenty of atmosphere.
spots/7/access: 15-minute walk uphill along Kitano-zaka from JR Sannomiya Station, or the Kitano Ijinkan stop on the City Loop bus
spots/7/hours: Mansions 09:00–17:00 or 18:00 (varies by mansion, to be confirmed)
spots/7/tip: You do not need to go into all of them; the Weathercock House and the Moegi House are enough. The Starbucks Kitano Ijinkan store at the foot of the hill (in a 1907 wooden mansion) only has seats if you go early in the morning.
spots/7/kid_tip: The long uphill walk is hard with a stroller. If your child gets tired, going only as far as Starbucks is fine.
spots/8/desc: The former home of a German trader, which has become the face of Ijinkan with its red brick walls and weathercock spire on the roof. It was closed from 2023 for seismic reinforcement work and has since reopened, so check once more whether it is open before you visit.
spots/8/access: Right in front of Kitano-cho Plaza
spots/8/closed: First Tuesday of June and February (to be confirmed)
spots/8/tip: The plaza in front is the center of the Ijinkan district, so you can still see it from outside even if it is under construction. A combined ticket with the neighboring Moegi House is available (to be confirmed).
spots/9/desc: A street-food lane counted among Japan's three great Chinatowns along with Yokohama and Nagasaki. The classic way to go around is to stand and eat butaman (pork buns), grilled squid and sweet-and-sour pork.
spots/9/access: 5-minute walk from JR/Hanshin Motomachi Station, 15-minute walk from Sannomiya Station
spots/9/tip: Roshoki's butaman has a long line, so it is better before 11:00 or around 15:00. Around Lunar New Year (Chunjie) it gets very crowded with lion dance events.
spots/9/kid_tip: Mild butaman and egg soup are safe choices for children. The lanes are narrow, so hold your child's hand.
spots/10/desc: A grid of streets that served as the foreign settlement after the port opened, where stone-built modern buildings now house luxury boutiques and cafes. It lies between Nankinmachi and Meriken Park, so you end up walking through naturally on the way.
spots/10/tip: The block behind the Daimaru Kobe store has the best atmosphere. In the evening the buildings are lit up, which is great for photos.
spots/11/desc: A shrine in the heart of the city with a 1,800-year history, where the downtown district begins right behind the red tower gate. The name Kobe (神戸) is said to come from this shrine's sacred estate (神戸).
spots/11/access: 5-minute walk from the west exit of JR Sannomiya Station
spots/11/tip: Stopping here on the way up to Kitano fits your route well. The charms for good relationships are famous.
spots/11/kid_tip: The small grove behind the grounds is nicely shaded and a good place for a short rest.
spots/12/name: Kobe Nunobiki Herb Garden and Ropeway
spots/12/desc: A 10-minute ropeway ride up from behind Shin-Kobe Station takes you to a mountaintop garden with herb fields, a glass greenhouse and German-style buildings. The terrace overlooks the whole city and harbor of Kobe, making it the easiest place in Kobe to see the night view.
spots/12/access: 5-minute walk to the ropeway's base station behind Shin-Kobe Station
spots/12/hours: Ropeway 09:30–16:45, with night service until 20:15 on weekends from spring to autumn and in summer (to be confirmed)
spots/12/closed: Closed twice a year for maintenance (to be confirmed)
spots/12/tip: Round trip ¥2,000 (admission included), and discounted night tickets are available after 17:00 (to be confirmed). On the way down, get off at the middle station and walk down toward Nunobiki Falls for a 30-minute stroll.
spots/12/kid_tip: The ropeway cabin is glass, so you can see right down below your feet. It is cooler up the mountain than in the city, so bring a jacket.
spots/13/desc: A viewing platform counted among Japan's three great night views along with Hakodate and Nagasaki. You climb by changing between a cable car and a ropeway, and the lights stretch out like a bow from Kobe to Osaka.
spots/13/access: From JR Rokkomichi Station or Hankyu Rokko Station, take city bus No. 18 to the Maya Cable-shita stop, then transfer to the cable car and ropeway
spots/13/hours: Cable car and ropeway 10:00–17:30, until 20:50 on Fri to Sun and holidays (to be confirmed)
spots/13/tip: In many seasons night service runs only Friday to Sunday, so plan around the day of the week. Round trip ¥1,560 (to be confirmed). There are almost no restaurants at the observatory, so eat before you go up.
spots/13/kid_tip: There is an indoor rest area where you can get out of the wind. Check the last ropeway time on your way up.
spots/14/desc: A viewing complex near the summit of Mt. Rokko, with European-style buildings, cafes and restaurants. On a clear day you can see all the way across Osaka Bay to Kansai Airport, and you can step inside the Rokko Shidare Observatory (separate fee), a round structure woven from wood.
spots/14/access: About 10 minutes by mountaintop bus from Rokko-sanjo Station on the Rokko Cable Car, or a 5-minute walk from Rokko-sanjo Station on the Rokko Arima Ropeway
spots/14/hours: 10:00–21:00 (varies by season and shop, to be confirmed)
spots/14/tip: Free entry; the Rokko Shidare Observatory costs ¥1,000 (to be confirmed). The summit is 5 to 7 degrees cooler than the city, so you need a jacket even in summer.
spots/14/kid_tip: There is a wide plaza and lawn that are great for running around, and with the restaurants gathered together you can even have dinner there.
spots/15/desc: An observatory right above the Rokko Cable Car's summit station, where the lights from Kobe's city center to Osaka Bay fit into a single view. It is right outside the cable car, so it is the easiest place to see the night view and then head back down.
spots/15/access: 1-minute walk from Rokko-sanjo Station on the Rokko Cable Car
spots/15/tip: It closes at 20:45 and the last cable car is around the same time, so check both. If you miss it, there is no good way to get down the mountain.
spots/15/kid_tip: There is an indoor cafe, so you can take photos outside and warm up inside.
spots/16/name: Rokko Mori-no-Oto Museum (formerly the Music Box Museum)
spots/16/desc: A museum of automatic musical instruments more than 100 years old, where staff wind the springs by hand and play them at set times. Outside is a garden path that follows a forest and pond, so an hour and a half passes quickly for both children and adults.
spots/16/access: About 10 minutes by mountaintop bus from Rokko-sanjo Station on the Rokko Cable Car, at the stop in front of the museum
spots/16/closed: Thursdays (except holidays and peak season, to be confirmed)
spots/16/tip: Arrive in time for a performance (around the top of each hour). Admission is ¥1,500 (to be confirmed), and a Mt. Rokko combined ticket gives a discount.
spots/16/kid_tip: Children watch the machines move on their own for a long time. The forest garden has a path for kids.
spots/17/desc: A mountaintop farm where sheep roam without fences, famous for the soft-serve ice cream and cheese made from the milk produced here. There are many slopes, so it is easier to think of the wide meadow, rather than the animals, as the main attraction.
spots/17/access: About 15 minutes by mountaintop bus from Rokko-sanjo Station on the Rokko Cable Car, or a 15-minute walk from Hoshi-no-Eki on the Maya Ropeway
spots/17/closed: Tuesdays (except holidays, varies by season, to be confirmed)
spots/17/tip: If you are not traveling with children, spending a relaxed time at Garden Terrace is the better choice. Admission is ¥500 (to be confirmed).
spots/17/kid_tip: Feeding the sheep and the soft-serve ice cream are the highlights. The terrain is easier with a baby carrier than a stroller.
spots/18/desc: A public bathhouse at Japan's oldest hot spring, over 1,300 years old, whose iron-rich water turns brown and is therefore called the Golden Bath. There is a free foot bath in front of the entrance, so you can enjoy the hot spring atmosphere without going into the bath.
spots/18/access: 5-minute walk from Arima-onsen Station on the Kobe Electric Railway, about 40 minutes by express bus from Sannomiya Bus Terminal
spots/18/closed: Second and fourth Tuesdays (next day if a holiday, to be confirmed)
spots/18/tip: Towel rental costs extra, so bring a small towel. Gin-no-Yu (the Silver Bath), a carbonated spring, is a 5-minute walk away, and a combined ticket for both is available (to be confirmed).
spots/18/kid_tip: Children in diapers cannot enter the bath. The water is hot, so keep children's baths short, about 10 minutes.
spots/19/name: Arima Onsen Street and Zuihoji Park
spots/19/desc: The heart of the hot spring town, where shops baking carbonated-spring senbei crackers and onsen manju buns line the narrow sloping lanes. Zuihoji Park behind the town has the most beautiful November maples in Arima.
spots/19/access: 5-minute walk from Arima-onsen Station, 15-minute walk to Zuihoji Park
spots/19/tip: Look for shops that hand you freshly baked carbonated senbei on the spot (such as Mitsumori). Arima cider is another specialty of this street.
spots/19/kid_tip: Some shops let you watch the senbei being baked through a glass window, and children stand there watching for a long time.
spots/20/desc: A World Heritage Site and the largest and most beautiful of Japan's castles to survive in their original form. Its white plaster walls look like an egret spreading its wings, which is why it is called the White Heron Castle. It is 40 minutes from Sannomiya by JR Special Rapid, so it makes a half-day trip.
spots/20/access: From the north exit of JR Himeji Station, 20-minute walk straight along Otemae-dori, or 5 minutes by bus
spots/20/hours: 09:00–17:00, last entry 16:00 (extended in summer, to be confirmed)
spots/20/tip: Since March 2026 the fee for foreign visitors has risen to ¥2,500 (¥1,000 for residents, to be confirmed). Buy the combined ticket with Koko-en at the entrance. During cherry blossom season and Golden Week, entry to the main keep is by numbered ticket.
spots/20/kid_tip: The stairs in the main keep are steep like ladders. Young children can be fine just seeing the 1st and 2nd floors, and the lawn outside the castle walls is great for running around.
spots/21/desc: An Edo-style garden next to the west side of Himeji Castle, made up of nine gardens divided by walls, with the scenery changing each time you pass through a gate. It is a good place to rest legs tired from the castle stairs by the pond.
spots/21/access: 5-minute walk from Otemon Gate of Himeji Castle
spots/21/hours: 09:00–17:00, last entry 16:30 (extended in summer, to be confirmed)
spots/21/tip: If you buy the combined ticket at the castle entrance, you do not have to wait in line twice. There is a teahouse inside where you can drink matcha.
spots/21/kid_tip: The pond is full of carp, and when you look down from the stone bridge they gather in a colorful swarm.
spots/22/desc: The gateway to Himeji, served by the JR Special Rapid and the Sanyo Shinkansen. Standing at the north exit, you can see the castle at the end of the main avenue straight ahead, so you cannot get lost. You can try anagomeshi and Himeji oden at the Fiore station building and the underground restaurant area.
spots/22/access: About 40 minutes by Special Rapid from JR Sannomiya Station, ¥1,010 (to be confirmed)
spots/22/tip: If you have lunch inside the station building on the way back from the castle, you can hop right on your train. Coin lockers are near the central ticket gate.
spots/23/name: Kobe Maritime Museum and Kawasaki Good Times World
spots/23/desc: The Kawasaki Heavy Industries exhibition hall is attached to the Maritime Museum, whose roof is shaped like white sails, and you can climb aboard real Shinkansen cars, helicopters and motorcycles. A child who loves vehicles will use up the full two hours.
spots/23/access: In Meriken Park, next to Port Tower
spots/23/closed: Mondays (next day if a holiday), year-end and New Year holidays
spots/23/tip: A Maritime Museum ticket includes Kawasaki Good Times World (to be confirmed). A combined ticket with Port Tower is a little cheaper.
spots/23/kid_tip: You can sit in the Shinkansen driver's seat, and there is an experience booth where you steer a ship into port. It is the number one pick for rainy days.
spots/24/desc: An indoor exhibit that layers media art over an aquarium, with lighting and music filling dark spaces. You go more for the light than for the fish, so two hours pass no matter what the weather is like.
spots/24/access: 18-minute walk from JR Sannomiya Station, 10-minute walk from Sannomiya-Hanadokemae Station on the Kaigan Subway Line
spots/24/tip: Around ¥2,400 on weekdays and ¥2,600 on weekends and holidays, a little more expensive, and a timed reservation is the safe choice (to be confirmed). You can see the harbor from the rooftop terrace.
spots/24/kid_tip: The spherical tank with light pouring down from the ceiling and the floor projections are a playground for children.
spots/25/desc: A zoo mostly housed in indoor greenhouses, so weather does not affect it, and where you get unusually close to the animals. Capybaras, sloths and birds roam without fences, and the flower-filled greenhouse is great for photos.
spots/25/access: Right at K Computer-mae (Animal Kingdom) Station on the Port Liner, about 14 minutes from Sannomiya
spots/25/hours: 10:00–17:00, last entry 16:30 (extended on weekends, to be confirmed)
spots/25/closed: Thursdays (except holidays and school vacations, to be confirmed)
spots/25/tip: It is on the way to the airport, so it fits well into the morning of your last day. Admission is ¥2,200 (to be confirmed).
spots/25/kid_tip: This is the number one pick for Kobe with children. Feeding experiences run at set times, so check the signboard at the entrance first.
spots/26/name: Akashi Kaikyo Bridge and Maiko Marine Promenade
spots/26/desc: A viewing walkway that runs inside the bridge structure beneath one of the world's longest suspension bridges, with a glass floor that shows the sea 47 m below. It is 20 minutes from Sannomiya by JR, so it suits a half-day outing.
spots/26/tip: On weekends and holidays the fee rises to around ¥500 (to be confirmed). Also see the neighboring Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall (free).
spots/26/kid_tip: If your child is scared of the glass floor, you can pass by on the walkway next to it.
spots/27/name: Sannomiya Center Gai and Daimaru Kobe
spots/27/desc: Kobe's main arcade, running from Sannomiya Station to Motomachi, where you can take care of meals and shopping all at once. In the basement of the Daimaru Kobe store at the end, you can buy gifts like Kobe pudding and cheesecake in one stop.
spots/27/access: Right outside the west exit of JR Sannomiya Station
spots/27/tip: The Daimaru basement has a bigger selection of gifts than the airport. Tax-free shopping is handled all at once at the counter inside Daimaru.
spots/27/kid_tip: It is an arcade, so rain is no problem, and one of the department stores along the way has a children's restroom.
spots/28/desc: A museum set up in an old brewery in Nada-Gogo, Japan's largest sake-producing region, where you can see the old tools and processes and enjoy a free tasting. Breweries such as Kikumasamune and Hamafukutsuru are within walking distance nearby.
spots/28/access: 5-minute walk from Hanshin Sumiyoshi Station, about 10 minutes from Sannomiya on the Hanshin line
spots/28/closed: Year-end and New Year holidays, Obon holidays (to be confirmed)
spots/28/tip: The museum alone takes 40 minutes, and visiting two or three breweries takes half a day. It is good for a trip of two adults or a rainy afternoon.
spots/28/kid_tip: Tasting is for adults only, and children are given amazake. The exhibits are short, so children may get bored.
spots/29/desc: An aquarium that newly opened in June 2024 and is the only place in western Japan where you can see an orca show. The Suma beach is right in front, so in summer you can combine it with swimming.
spots/29/access: 5-minute walk from JR Suma-kaihinkoen Station, about 15 minutes from Sannomiya
spots/29/tip: Prices differ between weekdays and weekends and rise further in peak season (around ¥3,100 to ¥3,700, to be confirmed). Check the orca show times first and plan your route around them.
spots/29/kid_tip: The front row of the show gets splashed. Bring a change of clothes for your child.
restaurants/0/desc: A good first-timer's Kobe beef restaurant, grilling Kobe beef on a teppan griddle right in front of you at lunch from ¥3,000. It is right in front of Sannomiya Station so the line is long, but tables turn over quickly and you will not wait long.
restaurants/0/tips/0: Lunch set costs half the dinner price
restaurants/1/desc: A Kobe beef specialty restaurant founded in 1885, with courses grilled by the chef in front of you starting from ¥10,000. It is a popular choice for a dinner on a special day, and there are several branches.
restaurants/2/cuisine: Kobe beef and Hyogo ingredients on the teppan
restaurants/2/desc: A teppanyaki restaurant run by the Hyogo agricultural cooperative, so the Kobe beef pedigree labeling is reliable. It is quiet and formal, which suits a commemorative dinner for two adults.
restaurants/3/desc: A shop that started in Kobe, serving a rice bowl piled mountain-high with roast beef, topped with yogurt sauce and an egg yolk. At around ¥1,500, it is good when you want a lighter meat meal instead of Kobe beef.
restaurants/3/tips/1: Large portions, good for sharing with a child
restaurants/4/desc: The original shop that has been making butaman in Nankinmachi since 1915, serving small, chewy buns that you eat standing up. The line is long, but it moves quickly and you will get yours in around 15 minutes.
restaurants/4/closed: Mondays (next day if a holiday, to be confirmed)
restaurants/5/desc: You can try Akashi's specialty, octopus egg balls dipped in warm dashi broth, at Sannomiya Center Plaza. The sauce is mild and gentle rather than spicy, so children eat it well too.
restaurants/5/tips/0: One plate (20 pieces) per person, around ¥1,000
restaurants/6/desc: A teppan shop in Nagata, considered the birthplace of sobameshi, Kobe's everyday dish of yakisoba stir-fried together with rice. You eat it topped with bokkake, simmered beef tendon, and it is 10 minutes from Sannomiya by train.
restaurants/6/tips/1: Few seats, so avoid the lunch peak
restaurants/7/desc: A leading shop for Kobe-style gyoza dipped in a miso-based sauce. A plate costs around ¥500, so it is good for a light bite before dinner. It is a small counter-style shop that suits two adults.
restaurants/7/tips/1: Almost nothing on the menu besides gyoza
restaurants/8/desc: A name synonymous with Kobe coffee, founded in 1948, and the Kitano-zaka branch is a two-story building with the feel of an old mansion. It is a good place to rest before or after walking Ijinkan, and it also has a breakfast set.
restaurants/9/desc: A bakery cafe in an old church building, famous for its sandwich lunch eaten under a high ceiling. It is between Shin-Kobe Station and Kitano, so it is a good stop on the way back from Herb Garden.
restaurants/9/tips/1: Buy cookies as gifts on the 1st floor
restaurants/10/desc: Kobe's signature dessert cafe, housed in Building No. 15 of the Old Foreign Settlement (the former American consulate). It is on the way to Meriken Park, so it suits an afternoon snack.
restaurants/11/desc: A famous Kobe cafe known for its warm, slightly salty cheesecake, topped with cheese and melted in the oven. It is close to the entrance of Nankinmachi, so it is a good dessert stop after eating there.
restaurants/11/tips/1: Takeaway comes in a paper box
restaurants/12/desc: Founded in 1923 and considered a pioneer of Kobe Western-style dining, with long-simmered beef stew and charcoal-grilled steak as its signature dishes. It suits two adults for a calm dinner as an alternative to Kobe beef teppanyaki.
restaurants/12/tips/1: The lunch stew set is good value
restaurants/13/desc: An everyday Kobe Western-style restaurant that has been running since 1952, with demi-glace omurice and beef cutlet at around ¥1,500. It is one train stop from Harborland, so it combines well as a lunch spot.
restaurants/14/desc: The home of tansan senbei, thin crackers baked with Arima hot spring water, where you can watch them being baked through a glass window. They hand you the fresh ones on the spot and also sell tins as gifts.
restaurants/14/tips/0: Freshly baked ones are limited in quantity
restaurants/15/signature: Soba set and Kobe beef rice bowl
restaurants/15/desc: A cozy restaurant on the onsen street serving soba and udon set meals and a Kobe beef rice bowl for around ¥2,000. It has both floor seating and tables, so it is an easy choice with children after the hot spring.
restaurants/16/signature: Mt. Rokko view pasta and dessert
restaurants/16/desc: A viewing cafe inside Rokko Garden Terrace, where a window seat looks down over the city of Kobe and Osaka Bay. It is the most convenient place to have dinner before the night view.
restaurants/16/closed: None (shorter hours in winter, to be confirmed)
restaurants/16/tips/0: Expect a wait for window seats at dusk
restaurants/17/cuisine: Western food and Kobe beef dishes
restaurants/17/desc: A restaurant with a view inside Rokko Garden Terrace, with a good range of family dishes such as hamburger steak, curry and udon. The hall is spacious, so it is easy to come in with a stroller.
restaurants/17/closed: None (shorter hours in winter, to be confirmed)
restaurants/17/tips/0: The largest space in Garden Terrace
restaurants/18/desc: A restaurant specializing in rice bowls topped with grilled conger eel, a specialty of the sea off Himeji, close to Himeji Station. It is a good lunch on the way back from the castle, and the soft flesh is fine for children too.

restaurants/21/tips/0: Expect a wait for window seats at dusk
restaurants/21/tips/1: You can go without picking a shop in advance

hotels/0/desc: A hotel chain with a natural hot spring public bath and free late-night soba noodles, 5 minutes on foot from Motomachi Station, Nankinmachi and the Old Foreign Settlement. It is good for relaxing tired legs after a day trip to Arima or Rokko, and satisfaction is high for both two women traveling together and families.
hotels/0/pts/0: Walk to Nankinmachi and Meriken Park
hotels/1/desc: A rebuilt version of Kobe's landmark hotel, which opened in 1870, now set on the stone-paved streets of the Old Foreign Settlement, with spacious rooms and a famous breakfast buffet. The lobby and bar have a distinctly Kobe atmosphere, and it is a 5-minute walk from Motomachi Station.
hotels/1/pts/0: In the middle of the Old Foreign Settlement
hotels/2/desc: A 35-story hotel standing in Meriken Park, where the Port Tower and Harborland night views spread out below the window from the upper-floor rooms. There is a shuttle bus to Sannomiya, and if you choose a harbor-side room you do not even need to go out for a night walk.
hotels/2/pts/1: Right in front of Meriken Park
hotels/3/desc: A large hotel attached to Shimin-Hiroba Station on the Port Liner, on one line connecting the Animal Kingdom and Kobe Airport. It has indoor and outdoor pools and family rooms, and Sannomiya is 10 minutes away by free shuttle and the Port Liner.
hotels/3/pts/0: Close to Animal Kingdom and the airport
hotels/4/desc: A business hotel 5 minutes east of Sannomiya Station, with a simple breakfast included. The rooms are small but clean, and it is close to the bus terminal, so getting to Arima and the airport is easy.
hotels/5/desc: A large ryokan-style hotel at Arima Onsen, where the open-air bath on the top floor lets you enjoy both the Golden and Silver hot springs while looking at the foothills of Mt. Rokko. You can choose between a buffet and kaiseki, and there is a children's play area, so it is also fine for families.
hotels/5/pts/0: Golden and Silver springs in the rooftop open-air bath
hotels/6/desc: An adults-only luxury ryokan in the middle of the onsen street, where every room's meal is served as kaiseki in a private dining room. Children under 13 are not accepted, so it suits a commemorative trip for two adults.
hotels/6/pts/1: In-room dining and Golden and Silver springs

bplan/0/desc: An indoor alternative near the harbor for rainy days or when the mountaintop viewpoints are closed. The experience is built on lighting, so it does not depend on the weather.
bplan/1/desc: A substitute for Port Tower when you are going with a child who loves vehicles. It is closed on Mondays, so go to Atoa on that day.
bplan/2/desc: A substitute when the Himeji Castle day trip is too much for a child. It is on the Port Liner on the way to the airport, so it also fits the morning of your last day.
bplan/3/desc: For when Animal Kingdom is closed on a Thursday or you want to see the orca show. In summer you can combine it with swimming at the beach out front.
bplan/4/desc: For adults on a rainy afternoon or when you have a half day free. It is 10 minutes from Sannomiya by Hanshin train, and tastings are free.
bplan/5/desc: A stop on the way if you are driving a rental car to Awaji Island. It is also 20 minutes by train, so it is good when you have a free half day.
bplan/6/desc: A night view alternative when the Rokko Cable Car is closed for maintenance. However, the Maya Cable Car is also closed on Tuesdays, and night service is mostly Friday to Sunday.
bplan/7/desc: For when the Herb Garden ropeway is closed or you have time to spare: a 15-minute walk from behind Shin-Kobe Station. Free.
nearby_alternatives/0/reason: You fly into the same Kansai Airport, and Osaka has more food and theme parks such as Dotonbori and Universal Studios, while Kobe can be added as a day trip.
nearby_alternatives/1/reason: If traditional scenery such as temples, gardens and kimono strolls is your goal, Kyoto is the place, and Kobe's night view can be added as a day outing.
nearby_alternatives/2/reason: If you liked Himeji Castle, Kurashiki Bikan Historical Quarter and Korakuen are an hour away by Shinkansen and far less crowded.
nearby_alternatives/3/reason: If hot springs are the main purpose, Beppu and Yufuin offer a wider variety of baths and places to stay than Arima.
